query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of a high atomic size mismatch element (e.g., a rare‐earth element such as yttrium) to phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys will improve their glass‐forming ability and enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
generation.material_initial_state: Phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy or compositionally complex alloys that, when processed conventionally, tend to crystallize upon cooling and exhibit a narrow supercooled liquid region.
generation.intervention: Introduce a small concentration (on the order of 1–3 at.%) of a rare‐earth element like yttrium into the base alloy composition.
generation.conditions: The intervention is expected to be effective under conditions of comparable cooling rates (e.g., melt spinning or rapid quenching) that usually produce a metastable amorphous phase. Its beneficial effect may diminish if the concentration is too high (leading to secondary phase formation) or if cooling is too rapid or too slow relative to the critical cooling rate.
generation.structural_mediator: The added element is anticipated to increase chemical and topological disorder and promote atomic packing frustration, which can—in turn—increase the nucleation barrier for crystallization.
generation.mechanism: Yttrium atoms, due to their size mismatch relative to the other constituent atoms, are expected to induce local lattice distortions and increase the energy barrier for crystal nucleation. This inhibits the growth of crystalline phases during cooling and enhances the stability of the amorphous structure by retarding atomic mobility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline phosphorus‐containing alloy without the rare‐earth addition, the modified alloy should exhibit a wider supercooled liquid region, a higher glass transition temperature (Tg) and crystallization onset temperature (Tx), as well as a lower critical cooling rate required for glass formation.
generation.baseline: Phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys processed under standard conditions without the yttrium (or similar) addition, which typically show limited glass‐forming ability and lower thermal stability against crystallization.
generation.boundary: The intervention may not work if the rare‐earth content exceeds the optimal level (leading to unwanted second phases), if the base alloy’s composition lies outside the range where atomic size mismatch can be effectively leveraged, or if processing conditions (e.g., extreme cooling rates) override the nucleation inhibition effect.
generation.uncertainty: The precise improvement in thermal stability and the optimal dopant concentration remain uncertain, as the effect may depend on the detailed chemistry and processing conditions of the phosphorus‐containing alloy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloy and a second set with a 1–3 at.% addition of yttrium. Process both sets using controlled melt-spinning to induce amorphization. Characterize the samples by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to measure Tg, Tx, and the width of the supercooled liquid region; employ X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to assess the amorphous versus crystalline phase fractions; determine the critical cooling rate for glass formation.
measurements: DSC for glass transition and crystallization temperatures
XRD for phase identification and quantification of amorphous content
Measurement of critical cooling rate via controlled cooling experiments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yttrium-doped samples do not show a statistically significant increase in the supercooled liquid region width, higher Tg/Tx, or a reduced critical cooling rate compared to the baseline samples, then the hypothesis that the minor addition improves both the glass-forming ability and thermal stability of the amorphous state will be considered falsified.

Question: How does the addition of Cr to the HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy affect its phase composition, microstructure, and room-temperature mechanical properties, specifically regarding the synergy between strength and ductility?. System: HfMoTaTiZr (30.0 at% Hf, 16.1 at% Mo, 30.4 at% Ta, 8.1 at% Ti, 15.4 at% Zr) and HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 (28.8 at% Hf, 15.5 at% Mo, 29.1 at% Ta, 7.7 at% Ti, 14.7 at% Zr, 4.2 at% Cr). Processing: Vacuum arc melting in an inert gas atmosphere; ingots re-melted at least 5 times to improve chemical homogeneity; weight loss did not exceed 0.5 wt%. Test conditions: Room temperature; Vickers hardness with 0.3 kg load and 15 s dwelling time; compression tests on cylindrical samples (3 mm diameter, 6 mm height) at a ram speed of 0.008 mm s−1 (strain rate 0.001/s).
